claim: Axons fail to regenerate after central nervous system (CNS) injury.
source: Axons fail to regenerate after central nervous system (CNS) injury.
evidence: This is a well-established statement in the field, supported by general scientific knowledge.

claim: Modulation of the PTEN/mTORC1 pathway in retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) promotes axon regeneration after optic nerve injury.
source: Modulation of the PTEN/mTORC1 pathway in retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) promotes axon regeneration after optic nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: AKT activation, downstream of Pten deletion, promotes axon regeneration.
source: Here, we report that AKT activation, downstream of Pten deletion, promotes axon regeneration and RGC survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 showing increased axon regeneration with AKT activation.

claim: AKT activation promotes RGC survival.
source: Here, we report that AKT activation, downstream of Pten deletion, promotes axon regeneration and RGC survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E-F showing increased RGC survival with AKT activation.

claim: GSK3β plays an indispensable role in mediating AKT-induced axon regeneration.
source: We further demonstrate that GSK3β plays an indispensable role in mediating AKT-induced axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that constitutive activation of GSK3β reduces AKT-induced axon regeneration (Figure 2).

claim: Deletion or inactivation of GSK3β promotes axon regeneration independently of the mTORC1 pathway.
source: Deletion or inactivation of GSK3β promotes axon regeneration independently of the mTORC1 pathway, whereas constitutive activation of GSK3β reduces AKT-induced axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that rapamycin treatment does not affect GSK3β deletion-induced axon regeneration (Figure 4).

claim: Constitutive activation of GSK3β reduces AKT-induced axon regeneration.
source: Deletion or inactivation of GSK3β promotes axon regeneration independently of the mTORC1 pathway, whereas constitutive activation of GSK3β reduces AKT-induced axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C-D showing reduced axon regeneration with GSK3β S9A expression.

claim: eIF2Bε is a novel downstream effector of GSK3β in regulating axon regeneration.
source: Importantly, we have identified eIF2Bε as a novel downstream effector of GSK3β in regulating axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that eIF2Bε inhibition reduces GSK3β-mediated axon regeneration (Figure 5).

claim: Inactivation of eIF2Bε reduces both GSK3β and AKT-mediated effects on axon regeneration.
source: Inactivation of eIF2Bε reduces both GSK3β and AKT-mediated effects on axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6 showing reduced axon regeneration with eIF2Bε E572A expression.

claim: Constitutive activation of eIF2Bε is sufficient to promote axon regeneration.
source: Constitutive activation of eIF2Bε is sufficient to promote axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing increased axon regeneration with eIF2Bε S535A expression.

claim: The AKT-GSK3β-eIF2Bε signaling module plays a key role in regulating axon regeneration in the adult mammalian CNS.
source: Our results reveal a key role of the AKT-GSK3β-eIF2Bε signaling module in regulating axon regeneration in the adult mammalian CNS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Axon injury in the adult mammalian CNS causes irreversible damages and permanent loss of functions due to a diminished intrinsic regenerative capability of mature CNS neurons and an inhibitory extrinsic environment.
source: Axon injury in the adult mammalian central nervous system (CNS) causes irreversible damages and permanent loss of functions due to a diminished intrinsic regenerative capability of the mature CNS neurons as well as an inhibitory extrinsic environment (Horner and Gage, 2000; Yiu and He, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reactivation of the intrinsic regenerative capability promotes CNS axon regeneration after injury.
source: Reactivation of the intrinsic regenerative capability promotes CNS axon regeneration after injury (Fischer et al., 2004; Gaub et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2009; O'Donovan et al., 2014; Park et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2009; Watkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of PTEN in adult retinal ganglion cells promotes axon regeneration after optic nerve injury.
source: Significantly, deletion of PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) in adult retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) promotes axon regeneration after optic nerve injury (Park et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of PTEN leads to the accumulation of PIP3, resulting in the activation of AKT via PDK1-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Loss of PTEN leads to the accumulation of PIP3 (phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate), resulting in the activation of the serine/threonine kinase AKT via PDK1-mediated phosphorylation (Carnero et al., 2008; Luo et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work describing the PTEN/AKT signaling pathway.

claim: AKT is a critical node in cell signaling downstream of growth factors, cytokines, and other cellular stimuli and regulates a wide spectrum of cellular functions, including cell survival, growth, proliferation, metabolism, and migration.
source: AKT is a critical node in cell signaling downstream of growth factors, cytokines, and other cellular stimuli and regulates a wide spectrum of cellular functions, which include cell survival, growth, proliferation, metabolism, and migration (Manning and Cantley, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) plays an important role in mediating Pten deletion-induced axon regeneration.
source: Activation of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) plays an important role in mediating Pten deletion-induced axon regeneration (Park et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: mTORC1-independent pathway(s) may exist to regulate axon regrowth in Pten-deficient neurons.
source: However, mTORC1-independent pathway(s) may exist to regulate axon regrowth in the Pten-deficient neurons because 1) pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin treatment only partially neutralizes the effects of Pten deficiency on axon regeneration (Park et al., 2008); 2) genetic ablation of TSC1 (tuberous sclerosis complex 1), a negative regulator of mTORC1, or manipulation of downstream effectors of mTORC1 only partially but not completely recapitulated the axon regeneration effects mediated by Pten deletion (Park et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited prior work showing incomplete effects of mTORC1 manipulation.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin treatment only partially neutralizes the effects of Pten deficiency on axon regeneration.
source: pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin treatment only partially neutralizes the effects of Pten deficiency on axon regeneration (Park et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Genetic ablation of TSC1 or manipulation of downstream effectors of mTORC1 only partially but not completely recapitulated the axon regeneration effects mediated by Pten deletion.
source: genetic ablation of TSC1 (tuberous sclerosis complex 1), a negative regulator of mTORC1, or manipulation of downstream effectors of mTORC1 only partially but not completely recapitulated the axon regeneration effects mediated by Pten deletion (Park et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GSK3 is a signal transducer of AKT.
source: GSK3 (glycogen synthase kinase 3) is a signal transducer of AKT.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of cell signaling.

claim: The GSK3 family consists of two members in mammals: GSK3α and GSK3β.
source: In mammals, the GSK3 family consists of two members, GSK3α and GSK3β.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: AKT inactivates the kinase activity of GSK3 through phosphorylation of GSK3α at Ser21 or GSK3β at Ser9.
source: AKT inactivates the kinase activity of GSK3 through phosphorylation of GSK3α at Ser21 or GSK3β at Ser9 (Cross et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Using Gsk3a-S21A/Gsk3b-S9A double knock-in mice, one group did not observe obvious phenotype in sensory axon regeneration.
source: Using Gsk3a-S21A/Gsk3b-S9A double knock-in mice, in which GSK3α/GSK3β cannot be inactivated by AKT-mediated phosphorylation, one group did not observe obviously phenotype in sensory axon regeneration (Zhang et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Sustained GSK3 activity markedly facilitated sciatic nerve regeneration in Gsk3a-S21A/Gsk3b-S9A double knock-in mice.
source: whereas the other group reported that sustained GSK3 activity markedly facilitated sciatic nerve regeneration (Gobrecht et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of GSK3 by lithium administration stimulates axon formation and elongation in the presence or absence of inhibitory substrates after spinal cord injury.
source: In the CNS, pharmacological inactivation of GSK3 by the administration of lithium, a GSK3 inhibitor, stimulates axon formation and elongation in the presence or absence of inhibitory substrates after spinal cord injury (Dill et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mechanism of lithium action is not completely clear as many other potential targets including a number of vital enzymes are also inhibited by lithium in an uncompetitive manner.
source: However, the mechanism of lithium action is not completely clear as many other potential targets including a number of vital enzymes are also inhibited by lithium in an uncompetitive manner (Phiel and Klein, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: AKT activation was readily detectable in RGCs in the developing retina and was significantly reduced in adult mice.
source: AKT activation, indicated by phosphorylation at Ser473 (Bozulic and Hemmings, 2009), was readily detectable in RGCs labeled by anti-Tuj1 immunoreactivity in the developing retina and was significantly reduced in adult mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Deletion of Pten leads to increased phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473 in RGCs.
source: Two weeks after viral injection, we detected increased phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473 in RGCs either with or without ONC, in comparison with Ptenf/fmice injected with AAV-GFP as a control (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A–B.

claim: Expression of constitutively active AKT promotes robust axon regeneration after optic nerve crush.
source: While very few axon fibers extended beyond the crush site in the AAV-GFP injected control, robust axon regeneration was stimulated in the AAV-caAKT injected retina (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Upon AKT activation, many regenerating axon fibers were observed at the proximal region of the crush site, and the number of regenerating axons gradually declined over a longer distance from the lesion site.
source: Upon AKT activation, many regenerating axon fibers were observed at the proximal region of the crush site. The number of regenerating axons gradually declined over a longer distance from the lesion site (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In comparison to 25.7% of RGCs remaining in the AAV-GFP injected control, significantly more RGCs (48.4%) were scored in the AAV-caAKT injected retina two weeks after ONC.
source: In comparison to 25.7% of RGCs remaining in the AAV-GFP injected control, significantly more RGCs (48.4%) were scored in the AAV-caAKT injected retina (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Pten deletion activates AKT.
source: Our results indicate that Pten deletion activates AKT, and AKT activation promotes both axon regeneration and RGC survival after optic nerve injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased phospho-AKT in Pten-deleted RGCs.

claim: Rapamycin treatment partially reduced the number of regenerating axon fibers in AAV-caAKT-injected retinas.
source: In comparison with the vehicle treatment as a control, rapamycin treatment partially reduced the number of regenerating axon fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: AKT-induced RGC survival was largely neutralized by rapamycin treatment.
source: AKT-induced RGC survival was largely neutralized by rapamycin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: Phospho-GSK3β level was higher in the developing retina relative to the adult age.
source: Phospho-GSK3β level was higher in the developing retina relative to the adult age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AAV-caAKT injection increased phosphorylation of GSK3β at Ser9 in RGCs.
source: Two weeks after AAV-caAKT injection in adult wild-type mice, we detected increased phosphorylation of GSK3β at Ser9 in RGCs either with or without ONC, in comparison with the AAV-GFP injected retina as a control (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–B.

claim: Pten deletion led to increased phosphorylation of GSK3β at Ser9 in RGCs.
source: As expected, increased phosphorylation of GSK3β was observed in Pten-deficient RGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GSK3β is a downstream target of PTEN/AKT signaling in RGCs.
source: Our results indicate that GSK3β is a downstream target of PTEN/AKT signaling in RGCs.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing increased GSK3β phosphorylation with AKT activation and Pten deletion.

claim: Co-injection of AAV-GSK3β S9A with AAV-caAKT significantly reduced regenerative axon growth compared to AAV-caAKT and AAV-GFP co-injection.
source: In comparison with the AAV-caAKT and AAV-GFP co-injection, regenerative axon growth was significantly reduced by AAV-GSK3β S9A co-injection (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C–D.

claim: AKT-induced RGC survival was not affected by the expression of GSK3β S9A.
source: However, AKT-induced RGC survival was not affected by the expression of GSK3β S9A (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: AKT phosphorylates and inactivates GSK3β, leading to improved axon regeneration, but not RGC survival.
source: Our results indicate that AKT phosphorylates and thus inactivates GSK3β, leading to improved axon regeneration, but not RGC survival.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that GSK3β S9A blocks AKT-induced axon regeneration but not survival.

claim: Gsk3b deletion resulted in improved axon regeneration after optic nerve crush.
source: While no obvious regenerating axon fibers were observed in the AAV-GFP injected control, Gsk3b deletion resulted in improved axon regeneration (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 1 day after ONC, optic nerve fibers terminated at the crush site in Gsk3bf/f mice injected with either AAV-GFP or AAV-Cre.
source: At 1 day after ONC, optic nerve fibers terminated at the crush site in Gsk3bf/f mice injected with either AAV-GFP or AAV-Cre.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the time course analysis.

claim: At 3 days after ONC, axon sprouting was observed in Gsk3b-deleted RGCs.
source: At 3 days after ONC, we observed axon sprouting in the Gsk3b-deleted RGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the time course analysis.

claim: At 7 days after ONC, regenerating axon fibers extended beyond the lesion site in Gsk3b-deficient RGCs, overcoming the inhibitory environment at the lesion site.
source: At 7 days after ONC, regenerating axon fibers extended beyond the lesion site in Gsk3b-deficient RGCs, overcoming the inhibitory environment at the lesion site labeled by immunohistochemistry for chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan (CSPG) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the time course analysis.

claim: Deletion of Gsk3a did not stimulate the regenerative response of injured axons.
source: However, deletion of Gsk3a did not stimulate the regenerative response of injured axons (Figure 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AKT activation increased phosphorylation of GSK3α at Ser21.
source: although AKT activation also increased its phosphorylation at Ser21 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: AAV-GSK3β K85A injection resulted in many regenerating axon fibers extending beyond the lesion site two weeks after ONC.
source: Two weeks after ONC, we observed many regenerating axon fibers extending beyond the lesion site in the AAV-GSK3β K85A injected mice, a regenerative response slightly weaker in comparison with Gsk3b deletion (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Gsk3a deletion, Gsk3b deletion, and AAV-GSK3β K85A injection did not change the rate of RGC survival two weeks after ONC.
source: None of these manipulations changed the rate of RGC survival (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,D.

claim: The deletion of Gsk3b, but not Gsk3a, promotes RGC axon regeneration likely through inactivation of the kinase activity of GSK3β.
source: Our results indicate that the deletion of Gsk3b, but not Gsk3a, promotes RGC axon regeneration likely through inactivation of the kinase activity of GSK3β.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that both Gsk3b deletion and kinase-dead GSK3β promote axon regeneration.

claim: AKT activation significantly increased mTORC1 activity in RGCs.
source: While AKT activation significantly increased the mTORC1 activity, evidenced by a higher fluorescence intensity of p-S6 immunoreactivity in RGCs in adult wild-type mice injected with AAV-caAKT compared to the control injection, Gsk3b deletion did not perturb the activity of mTORC1 as the immunofluorescence intensity of p-S6 remained at the same low level as the control (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Gsk3b deletion did not perturb the activity of mTORC1.
source: While AKT activation significantly increased the mTORC1 activity, evidenced by a higher fluorescence intensity of p-S6 immunoreactivity in RGCs in adult wild-type mice injected with AAV-caAKT compared to the control injection, Gsk3b deletion did not perturb the activity of mTORC1 as the immunofluorescence intensity of p-S6 remained at the same low level as the control (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: Gsk3b deficiency-induced axon regeneration was not affected by rapamycin treatment.
source: While rapamycin markedly reduced AKT-induced axon regeneration and RGC survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), Gsk3b deficiency-induced axon regeneration was not affected by rapamycin treatment, and neither was RGC survival in Gsk3b-deleted RGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin significantly reduced Gsk3b deletion induced axon regeneration.
source: However, treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin significantly reduced Gsk3b deletion induced axon regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: GSK3β-mediated effects on axon regeneration require protein synthesis but are achieved through an mTORC1-independent mechanism.
source: Our results indicate that GSK3β-mediated effects on axon regeneration require protein synthesis but are achieved through an mTORC1-independent mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that anisomycin but not rapamycin blocks GSK3β-mediated axon regeneration.

claim: eIF2B is a heteropentameric guanine nucleotide exchange factor that converts eIF2 from the inactive GDP–bound form to the active GTP-bound complex, representing a rate-limiting step in protein translation initiation.
source: eIF2B (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B) is a heteropentameric guanine nucleotide exchange factor that converts eIF2 (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2) from the inactive GDP–bound form to the active GTP-bound complex, representing a rate-limiting step in protein translation initiation (Campbell et al., 2005; Pavitt, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: eIF2Bε is inhibited by GSK3β phosphorylation at the Ser535 site.
source: eIF2Bε (eIF2B epsilon subunit), the largest catalytic subunit of eIF2B, is inhibited by GSK3β phosphorylation at the Ser535 site, linking regulation of global protein synthesis to GSK3β signaling (Pap and Cooper, 2002; Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2Bε at Ser535 in RGCs was significantly higher in adult mice in comparison with that in the developing retina.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2Bε at Ser535 in RGCs was significantly higher in adult mice in comparison with that in the developing retina (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: eIF2Bε-controlled protein translation is maintained at a low basal level in adult RGCs.
source: indicating that elF2Bε-controlled protein translation is maintained at a low basal level in adult RGCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the high phosphorylation of eIF2Bε in adult RGCs.

claim: Optic nerve injury alone did not activate eIF2Bε.
source: Optic nerve injury alone did not activate eIF2Bε as the phosphorylation of eIF2Bε was detected at similar levels to uninjured retinas after ONC (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Phospho-eIF2Bε (Ser535) immunoreactivity was markedly reduced in Gsk3b-deleted RGCs in the presence or absence of axon injury.
source: By contrast, phospho-eIF2Bε (Ser535) immunoreactivity was markedly reduced in Gsk3b-deleted RGCs in the presence or absence of axon injury (Figure 5A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Gsk3b deletion results in increased eIF2Bε activity for protein translation.
source: indicating increased eIF2Bε activity for protein translation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduced phosphorylation of eIF2Bε in Gsk3b-deleted RGCs.

claim: Gsk3a deletion did not change eIF2Bε phosphorylation.
source: Gsk3a deletion did not change eIF2Bε phosphorylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: GSK3α may not regulate eIF2Bε activity in RGCs.
source: suggesting that GSK3α may not regulate eIF2Bε activity in RGCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of effect of Gsk3a deletion on eIF2Bε phosphorylation.

claim: The number of regenerating axons was significantly reduced by AAV-eIF2Bε E572A co-injection with AAV-Cre in Gsk3bf/f mice two weeks after ONC.
source: Two weeks after ONC, the number of regenerating axons was significantly reduced by AAV-eIF2Bε E572A co-injection (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C–D.

claim: Gsk3b deletion resulted in a significant increase in OPP-labeled newly synthesized proteins.
source: While the basal level of protein translation in RGCs was suppressed by treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin, Gsk3b deletion resulted in a significant increase in OPP-labeled new synthesized proteins, which was largely negated by eIF2Bε E572A treatment (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E–F.

claim: The increase in newly synthesized proteins from Gsk3b deletion was largely negated by eIF2Bε E572A treatment.
source: While the basal level of protein translation in RGCs was suppressed by treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin, Gsk3b deletion resulted in a significant increase in OPP-labeled new synthesized proteins, which was largely negated by eIF2Bε E572A treatment (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E–F.

claim: Protein synthesis is tightly controlled by GSK3β/eIF2Bε signaling during axon regeneration.
source: These results clearly demonstrate that protein synthesis is tightly controlled by GSK3β/eIF2Bε signaling during axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that eIF2Bε activity affects protein synthesis and axon regeneration.

claim: Inhibition of eIF2Bε had no effect on the survival of Gsk3b-deleted RGCs.
source: However, inhibition of eIF2Bε had no effect on the survival of Gsk3b-deleted RGCs (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G–H.

claim: The regenerative response stimulated by AAV-caAKT injection was significantly reduced by co-injection of AAV-eIF2Bε E572A at 2 weeks after ONC.
source: At 2 weeks after ONC, the regenerative response stimulated by AAV-caAKT injection was significantly reduced by co-injection of AAV-eIF2Bε E572A (Figure 6A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: AKT-induced RGC survival was not perturbed by eIF2Bε E572A inhibition.
source: while AKT-induced RGC survival was not perturbed by eIF2Bε E572A inhibition (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C–D.

claim: eIF2Bε is required for both AKT and GSK3β-mediated effects on axon regeneration, but plays a minimal role in RGC survival after axon injury.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that eIF2Bε is required for both AKT and GSK3β-mediated effects on axon regeneration, but plays a minimal role in RGC survival after axon injury.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that eIF2Bε inhibition blocks axon regeneration but not survival.

claim: Expression of eIF2Bε S535A significantly increased protein synthesis in RGCs compared with AAV-GFP injection.
source: As expected, expression of eIF2Bε S535A significantly increased protein synthesis in RGCs compared with AAV-GFP injection as a control (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A–B.

claim: Many regenerating axon fibers extending past the crush site were observed in the eIF2Bε S535A treated retinas at 2 weeks after ONC.
source: At 2 weeks after ONC, we observed many regenerating axon fibers extending past the crush site in the eIF2Bε S535A treated retinas (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C–D.

claim: The regenerative effect induced by eIF2Bε activation was reduced by protein synthesis inhibition with anisomycin treatment.
source: The regenerative effect induced by eIF2Bε activation was reduced by protein synthesis inhibition with anisomycin treatment, but was not affected by mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The regenerative effect induced by eIF2Bε activation was not affected by mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin treatment.
source: The regenerative effect induced by eIF2Bε activation was reduced by protein synthesis inhibition with anisomycin treatment, but was not affected by mTORC1 inhibition with rapamycin treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: mTORC1 signaling plays a minimal role in eIF2Bε-induced axon regeneration.
source: indicating that mTORC1 signaling plays a minimal role in eIF2Bε-induced axon regeneration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of effect of rapamycin on eIF2Bε-induced axon regeneration.

claim: AAV-eIF2Bε S535A injection did not change the rate of RGC survival at 2 weeks after ONC.
source: We further assessed whether activation of eIF2Bε affects neuronal survival at 2 weeks after ONC, and found that AAV-eIF2Bε S535A injection did not change the rate of RGC survival in comparison with the control injection (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E–F.

claim: Activation of eIF2Bε promotes axon regeneration with minimal effects on RGC survival.
source: These results demonstrate that activation of eIF2Bε promotes axon regeneration with minimal effects on RGC survival.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that eIF2Bε activation promotes axon regeneration but not survival.

claim: Both the inhibitory extrinsic environment and the diminished intrinsic regenerative capability in the adult CNS contribute to the poor regeneration of axons after injury.
source: Both the inhibitory extrinsic environment and the diminished intrinsic regenerative capability in the adult CNS contribute to the poor regeneration of axons after injury.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Removal of the inhibitory influences in the extracellular environment is insufficient to stimulate a major regenerative response.
source: Removal of the inhibitory influences in the extracellular environment is insufficient to stimulate a major regenerative response.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activation of intrinsic signaling pathways within CNS neurons has yielded encouraging results in promoting axon regeneration.
source: On the other hand, activation of intrinsic signaling pathways within CNS neurons has yielded encouraging results in promoting axon regeneration (de Lima et al., 2012; Kurimoto et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2011; Park et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: AKT was phosphorylated at Ser473 and thus activated in Pten-deleted RGCs.
source: We found that AKT was phosphorylated at Ser473 and thus activated in the Pten-deleted RGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased phospho-AKT in Pten-deleted RGCs.

claim: Expression of a constitutively active myristoylated AKT promoted both axon regeneration and RGC survival.
source: Significantly, expression of a constitutively active myristoylated AKT promoted both axon regeneration and RGC survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The mTORC1 pathway is an important downstream signaling in mediating Pten deletion-induced axon regeneration.
source: Previous studies have established that the mTORC1 pathway is an important downstream signaling in mediating Pten deletion-induced axon regeneration, as reactivation of this pathway by TSC1 deletion or S6K1 activation effectively promotes axon regeneration (Park et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reactivation of the mTORC1 pathway by TSC1 deletion or S6K1 activation effectively promotes axon regeneration.
source: as reactivation of this pathway by TSC1 deletion or S6K1 activation effectively promotes axon regeneration (Park et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: GSK3 signaling plays a role in developmental axon growth.
source: Several studies have demonstrated the role of GSK3 signaling in developmental axon growth (Hur et al., 2011; Hur and Zhou, 2010; Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the adult PNS, GSK3 signaling regulates mammalian sensory axon regeneration by inducing the expression of Smad1.
source: In the adult PNS, GSK3 signaling regulates mammalian sensory axon regeneration by inducing the expression of Smad1 (Saijilafu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the spinal cord injury model, neuronal deletion of Gsk3b enhances dorsal column axon regeneration via CRMP2-regulated microtubule dynamics, specifically in the growth cone.
source: In the spinal cord injury model, neuronal deletion of Gsk3b enhances dorsal column axon regeneration via CRMP2-regulated microtubule dynamics, specifically in the growth cone (Liz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GSK3α and GSK3β have been shown to act on different substrates in the brain.
source: Indeed GSK3α and GSK3β have been shown to act on different substrates in the brain (Soutar et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Complete elimination of GSK3 activity has been associated with the suppression of axon growth in developmental studies.

claim: Protein synthesis is primarily regulated at the initiation phase.
source: Protein synthesis is primarily regulated at the initiation phase, which involves binding of the methionyl–transfer RNA (Met–tRNAiMet) to the small 40s ribosomal subunit to form the 43 s pre-initiation complex, which then binds to an mRNA to form the 48 s pre-initiation complex that scans the AUG start codon.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of molecular biology.
